questions.explanation: The decision turns on what a lawful-tender statute does to the obligation, not on what a creditor prefers. Once Congress has declared the note lawful tender in payment of debts, a debtor who tenders it discharges the debt to the same extent as coin would, and a creditor who accepts it cannot afterwards claim the payment was insufficient. That is why the holding reaches a private sale between two merchants and is not confined to debts owed to the government. What the decision did not decide is whether Congress had the constitutional power to enact such a statute, which is the ground on which the same court divided two years later. questions.explanation: The striking thing about the silver dollar under the statutes of 1878 and 1890 is that it promised parity on its face and did not pay it in practice. The statutes and the coinage proclaimed the dollar at par with the gold dollar; the market, which had treated silver as a metal with its own price since the demonetisation of 1873, priced the bullion in the dollar far below. The Treasury met the paper it had issued out of the silver it had bought rather than out of gold, and the notes were redeemable in silver or in gold as the statute allowed. questions.explanation: The 1900 act consolidated rather than overturned. It named a unit, charged the Secretary with holding every other form of money at parity with it, and gave him the reserves and the authority to buy and sell in order to keep it there. From the report of a commission appointed to enquire into the financial crisis of 1907: the immediate occasion of the disturbance was the attempt of a syndicate to acquire the entire issue of the stock of one great industrial corporation. The syndicate had not paid for its contract and was compelled to borrow at the banks in order to complete the purchase; the borrowing was large, the security behind it was the stock in question, and the stock was falling. Several of the banks that had made the loans were in the position of owing more to their correspondents and depositors than they could in fact command in cash, and in the second week of October the calls against them came home in a volume that no single institution could meet. No currency of issue was in any danger, and the difficulty lay wholly in the credit of the borrowing banks.

questions.explanation: The shape of the 1908 act says a good deal about the state of the argument. It did two things that could be defended without settling anything: it let a bank in extremity issue paper against its own commercial paper, which is plainly an emergency measure, and it set up a bipartisan commission to report. Then it ended by limitation on a fixed date, so that Congress would have to decide the question again on the record rather than let the arrangement harden by silence. That is what a bridge looks like. The stronger and more popular claim, that the country needed a central bank and had only been waiting for a majority to admit it, fits the later course of events better than the act itself does, and the interesting historical question is why the emergency currency and the commission proved durable while the sunset did not.

questions.explanation: The commission's plan put the central bank in private hands, with a board representing the banks and the public at large, and that part did not survive. What survived was the central institution itself, the idea that a single body should hold the gold reserves and stand behind the reserves of the member banks, and the conviction that the earlier episodes of trouble had exposed a gap in the banking law. questions.explanation: The point the commission pressed is the one that carries the whole argument. A bank that was solvent when it opened on Monday could be insolvent by Friday, not because its own position had changed but because a depositor in another town had heard a rumour and had gone to the counter of the bank next door, and that bank's refusal to pay, rightly or wrongly, confirmed the rumour. A law that holds reserves against each bank separately will not touch that, because the failure is a failure of confidence and confidence does not answer to a percentage. What follows is a facility letting a solvent bank borrow on paper that is genuinely good, against reserves and gold held centrally, so that it need not sell what it has at ruinous prices to meet a demand it could otherwise meet. That is the recommendation the act of 1913 gave effect to, and the diagnosis is why the provision for elastic currency sits at the centre of the act rather than at its edge.

questions.explanation: The reform was always argued as though it were about notes because the note-issuing privilege was the only thing that made a federal charter worth having. A bank that issued no notes and did nothing else federally was a state bank with a federal name and an extra set of examinations and reports, and a good many sensible bankers saw no reason to accept that. So a proposal to make the federal charter exclusive was a proposal about who should be allowed to issue paper money, and the effects on lending and deposits followed from that rather than being the point of it. The honest way to put the argument is that the reform's proponents thought the country needed one note-issuing system and its opponents thought a country of state banks with a thin layer of national ones was a perfectly good arrangement, and that it happened to be the one they were used to. Neither position says much about credit, and both say a great deal about who should be trusted to promise.

questions.explanation: The order is forced by two different things having to happen in sequence. Coinage comes first, because a purchase law cannot mean anything while the mint will still coin the metal for anyone who brings it in at a fixed face value; demonetisation is what creates a market the government has to bid in. A monthly purchase with silver dollars issued in payment follows, and then a second and larger purchase law that issued notes redeemable at the Secretary's choice of metal rather than coin, which is the step that took the government into financing the metal itself. questions.explanation: Both of the chosen points are defects of the drafting rather than of the market, which is the test a critic of a statute has to meet. A statute that names a day and promises redemption on it has committed the government to a sum it has not yet got, and the act gave no mechanism for acquiring what it needed between its passage and the day; the danger the hard-money advocates pressed was exactly that the Treasury would be forced to buy at any price. And a figure expressed as a limit on what may be outstanding is a floor, because it forbids the government from contracting below it, so the act built a permanent stock of paper into the system by design. What the act did not do was create two kinds of paper, since a federal note was a federal note and any distinction between redeemable and irredeemable notes would have had to be made by a market judgement the act did not authorise; and private debts were already settled, since making the notes lawful tender was in force and the act left it there.

answer.exemplar: A strong answer says the minimum existed so the redemption machinery would deal with a manageable number of transactions instead of every single note, since the volume of paper in circulation was enormous and most of it was small. questions.explanation: The detail is small and it explains a great deal. If a holder may only present notes in sums of not less than a stated amount, then a person with a few dollars in his pocket cannot exercise the right, and the only people who can are those with a great many notes or those who collect them. That is the ordinary mechanics of a very large note issue and it was the answer to the obvious objection that a country with hundreds of millions of notes could not expect to process them one at a time. It is also, if you want a non-motive explanation of what happened in 1879, a large part of the explanation: the right existed, the day came, and the practical cost of using it exceeded what most people thought the note was worth. The act did not refuse to pay; it put a condition on the manner of presentation, and a condition on the manner is a real limit on what a promise is worth in practice.

questions.explanation: The rule answers fear, not credit. A bank that might not pay is a bank nobody will take notes from, and a bank nobody will take notes from is a bank nobody keeps an account with, whatever its assets are worth. So the rule says three things at once: pay in full, show that the signatures you pass are genuine, and if you cannot pay be suspended, which is an orderly and public fate rather than a private and secret one. The loss itself is neither shared nor reduced; the point is that the number of people who suddenly distrust a bank is bounded, because a suspension is a known event with a known end and everybody can see the rules being observed. A rule that merely postponed payment would have made the distrust worse, since it would have told every creditor that the clearing house itself doubted the money.

questions.explanation: The theory behind the districts is that a credit condition is local. A member bank knows its own customers, knows what the paper it is asked to discount was raised for, and is better placed than a board in Washington to say whether that paper is good. On that view the reserve bank is the point at which local knowledge meets national reserves, and the rate set in Washington supplies the tone while the district supplies the judgement. The assumption is contestable, and the act of 1935 is a good measure of how far it had been abandoned, since it gave a single committee the exclusive authority to direct the purchase and sale of securities for the whole system and required the district banks to comply, on the ground that the boundaries of a district are at most economic frontiers and not monetary ones. Whether the change settled that argument or postponed it is a live question.

questions.explanation: The reason is easy to state and easy to miss. Money does not observe district lines. If one reserve bank tightens while its neighbour does not, the effect leaks across the boundary through the clearing system and through the price of a bill drawn in one district and discounted in another. A system in which each district is a free agent therefore cannot deliver a national change in the quantity of credit, however well informed each district is. Giving one committee exclusive authority, and requiring the district banks to comply, is the step that makes a national policy possible, at the cost of the local autonomy the 1913 design had rested on. What the change did not settle is how much local knowledge the system could afford to lose, which is why the shape of the committee, with representatives chosen by the districts in regional groups, has been argued about ever since.

questions.explanation: The words are the whole content of the clause, and their force is easy to underestimate. A grant of power to buy and sell securities with no stated object invites the reading that the object is whatever the committee thinks is good, and on that reading a policy can be defended in terms of the level of security prices. A grant with a stated object has to be argued in terms of that object, and a programme that plainly did not accommodate trade could be challenged on the statute's own words. This is a familiar technique: give an authority a wide power and then name the purpose, so that the power is wide and the purpose is examinable. questions.explanation: The gold content of a dollar is the reciprocal of the price of an ounce in dollars. At 20.67 dollars an ounce a dollar held one twenty-sixty-seventh of an ounce, about 0.0484; at 35 dollars it holds one thirty-fifth, about 0.0286. The ratio of the second to the first is 20.67 divided by 35, which is 0.5906, so the gold content fell to about 59 per cent of its former amount and each dollar bought about 41 per cent less metal. Checked the other way, the price of gold rose from 20.67 to 35, a ratio of 1.6933, and one divided by 1.6933 is again 0.5906, the same fraction by a different route. The distractor that reports 41 per cent is the result of subtracting 0.5906 from one and then treating the size of the fall as though it were what remained, which is the classic way a devaluation figure gets stated backwards. The direction is worth being careful about: a higher dollar price for the same metal means each dollar buys less of it.

questions.explanation: Two ceilings doing two different jobs is the point. The first is a general rule: the government will not pay more for a fine ounce than the law says that ounce is worth, which keeps the programme from simply bidding the price up against itself. The second is a rule about a particular seller. Silver already in the country on the stated date was, in the drafters' view, not new supply but old stock, and a government that paid a premium for it would hand a windfall to whoever happened to be holding it at the moment the hoarding was ending. So the second limit caps what may be paid for that stock at rather less than half the monetary value and fixes a date for it, which makes it a rule about fairness to one class of holder rather than about the price of the metal. A reader who treats the two as one ceiling has missed that the act was deliberately buying new metal and deliberately refusing to pay up for old.

questions.explanation: Before 1935 the silver coins were an alloy in a ratio fixed in the nineteenth century and unrelated to the value of the metal, so the silver in a dollar of coins was worth very little and nobody would have hoarded it. questions.explanation: A statutory ratio promises that the two metals in the unit stand in a fixed relation, and it delivers that relation only while the market agrees. What happened to the silver in the dollar between the 1830s and the 1870s was that it became worth progressively less against the gold in it, which is a statement about two markets and not about the law. Once that has happened the two coins can no longer both be freely minted at the same face value, because whoever can get the dearer metal will melt down the coin made of the cheaper one, and the cheaper coin will disappear from circulation whether anyone voted for that or not. This is why free coinage of the silver dollar was stopped in 1873 and why the government had to become a buyer rather than a coiner. The unit did not change; the world's estimate of the two metals did, and the law was left holding a relation the market had abandoned.

questions.explanation: The asymmetry is the thing to be clear about. A bank holds a claim on its borrowers and owes a liability payable at the holder's convenience. The two have different dates and different certainties, and a run is the moment when the convenience of everybody exercising the liability coincides. Reserves do not prevent that; they determine how long a bank can meet a run before it must sell something, and selling quickly is what turns a temporary shortage into a permanent loss. That is why the two institutional answers of the period were not about the quality of a bank's management but about the behaviour of holders: a rule of disclosure about what a balance is, and a fund standing behind the balance so that a holder has something to be paid out of. The third and fourth options both take the run as a reason for doing nothing, which is the inference the whole reform was made to refuse.

questions.explanation: The distribution of the effect is exactly what a legal-tender statute is about, and it is why the question of the constitutionality of such a statute divided a court. A debtor benefits because a claim on the government is easier to obtain than coin, and because a larger supply of money means the creditor takes fewer real goods for the debt. A creditor is worse off in the same transaction, because the paper is worth less in goods than what it replaced, and the only thing standing between the creditor and that loss is a rule that says he must take it. The court that upheld the effect on a private sale in 1870 was therefore deciding which of two claims to a particular sum should win, and the statute said the creditor must take the paper if the debtor offered it. Whether Congress had the power to say so is a different question, and one that a court in the same decade answered both ways.

questions.explanation: The letter is reasoning from a balance sheet and the reasoning is the standard one. A farmer who owes more than he can see coming in, and who is paid in a money whose value he does not control, is a debtor in a contracting currency; a change that reduces the value of money reduces the number of bushels he must sell to clear a debt fixed in the old money, and it improves the position of every creditor whose claim was fixed in it. questions.explanation: The distinction is between a rule about what a creditor must accept and a rule about an obligation already fixed, and it is the distinction on which the sharpest objection to a legal-tender statute was pressed. A statute that says paper is lawful money in payment of debts is a rule about the discharge of an obligation, and it leaves it open whether it applies to a debt the parties had already fixed in a particular form. If the bargain was for a particular kind of money and the statute did not reach it, the debtor who tendered that money had paid, and the statute did not entitle him to substitute something else. That is why the 1870 decision was argued and why the same court a year later said the rule did not extend to a case in which the party owed gold. The two holdings sit together because the question in each case was the same one: does the statute reach this obligation.

questions.explanation: The instrument is a promise by the clearing house, secured on the balances the members have with it, and it buys time rather than safety. A member in trouble needs to convert a claim on another member into something it can pay with today, and the certificate does that; the loan it was given against, and the borrower behind that loan, are exactly as good and as bad as they were. That is why an issue of certificates could relieve a crisis without any new capital having entered the system, and why the relief was described at the time as an addition to the medium of circulation even though no metal moved. answer.exemplar: A strong answer says the two accounts are not rival descriptions of one act but rival claims about what the rate was for, and that they make different predictions about who issued notes afterwards. It should notice that the first has to explain why a revenue measure had the effect of keeping a system thin, and that the second has to explain why a measure with a revenue effect is described at all as though the money were incidental. It should avoid saying the second refutes the first, since a tax can be enacted for revenue and be relied on for its effect, and it should avoid treating the eventual disappearance of the tax as settling which was meant.

questions.explanation: The way to hold the two accounts is to ask what each predicts. If the tax were only a revenue measure, then the number of national banks would follow the number of men who wanted a federal charter, and the very smallness of that number would need a separate explanation, since the charter carried a note monopoly and the note business was the most profitable business a country bank had. If the tax was a barrier, then the smallness of the number is the measure of its success and the revenue was the cost of collecting it. Neither account can be proved from the statute alone, because a rate set high enough to exclude most banks is also a rate that raises a great deal of money from the few that issue, and that double character is precisely what makes the question hard. The interesting evidence is elsewhere, in the arguments of the people who wrote and repealed the provision, which is where a motive would show if one were recoverable at all.

questions.explanation: The argument is about what a holder is trusting, and it can be put in one sentence: a promise is a claim on a person and a coin is not. A person who is paid in a note has a claim on an institution whose solvency and intention he cannot observe, and every panic of the period is a crowd of people discovering that they did not know what they were holding. A coin puts an end to that dependence, because the holder can look at it, weigh it, and see that it is what it says. questions.explanation: The condition on presentation is what makes the answer a matter of degree rather than of kind. The statute created a right; it also created a minimum sum and a place, and between them they set the cost of using the right. questions.explanation: The order is forced by what each step required of the others and by the difference between stopping a thing and replacing it. Suspension came first, because the deposit insurance had nothing to insure if the notes behind a balance could not be exchanged for coin, and because the government could not negotiate a new price for the metal while the old parity was still promised. The temporary fund came next, since the point of suspending was to be able to reopen the banks, and a bank that reopens on the same terms as the bank that failed has told every depositor what to expect. The change in the law about the metal followed, once the government was off the old parity and could fix a new price, and the prohibition on private holding went with it because a price nobody may trade at is not a price. The general statute comes last, because its work was to make the emergency arrangement permanent and to deal with the machinery of credit, and a permanent scheme is not something a government constructs while it is still deciding what the emergency requires.

questions.explanation: The financing mechanism is doing something substantive, not merely raising the money. A promise by the treasury is a claim on the government's power to tax and borrow, and a depositor who has to rely on it is relying on a political process. A fund built out of assessments on the banks is a claim on a pool of assets that other banks have paid into, and the person whose confidence is being restored is being asked to trust his fellow bankers rather than his government. That is a real difference in what the word government means, and it is the reason a scheme financed that way can be described as insurance rather than as charity, since an insurance premium is exactly a payment into a pool by people who expect to be paid out of it. questions.explanation: Two hundred and forty-eight million over five hundred and thirty-four million is 0.4644, so about 46 per cent, and the complement of 54 per cent is what the other three sources contributed between them. Checked a second way, 534 minus 248 is 286, and 286 over 534 is 0.5356, the same remainder by subtraction. The 87 per cent in one distractor is 248 over 286, the certificate figure set against the other three sources only, and the 20 per cent is 106 over 534, the share of the imported gold. The interpretation follows from what the largest item is: clearing-house certificates were a promise by the clearing house, secured on the balances members had with it, and issuing them converted a claim on another member into something payable that day. Nearly half the relief was therefore a promise rather than a metal, which tells us the strain was in convertibility and not in the supply of coin, and it is why the reform that followed was about who could be trusted to make a promise in a crisis.

questions.explanation: The order is the sequence a crisis and its aftermath produce, and it is worth noticing that the two of the four steps that are not in the sequence are not part of this story at all, which is itself the point: the silver legislation and the panic it was followed by belong to a different question about what the currency was made of, and the reform of the note issue belongs to a different question about who could lend when the banks were closed. A reader who tries to place the silver repeal in the chain is being asked to connect two episodes that share a decade and almost nothing else. The three steps that do belong in the chain are forced by one another: an emergency measure buys time, a commission makes the argument in public and on the record, and a permanent system is what a country builds after it has been told, in detail, what it lacked.

answer.exemplar: A strong answer says the claim stopped being on one man and became on a class, because a failure was met out of a pool that every bank had paid into, so the depositor no longer had to be right about his own bank. It should notice that the sum insured was small, which shows the reform was aimed at the ordinary balance and not at the large one, and it should avoid claiming the risk was removed, since a deposit above the insured sum or in an uninsurable form remained exactly as exposed as before.

questions.explanation: The change is best described as a change in the identity of the debtor rather than in the amount of the promise. A depositor at an uninsured bank has a claim on a particular man, and that man's character, his neighbours' opinion of him, and the speed at which the news travels are all part of the value of the balance. An insured balance is a claim on a pool, and a pool is not frightened by the failure of one member, which is exactly the property the single bank could not have had. The small size of the insured sum is a useful corrective to any account that makes the reform sound like a guarantee of a large fortune: it was designed for the ordinary balance, and it is a measure of the judgement that an ordinary balance is what people move when a bank looks shaky. Above that sum, and in forms the law did not cover, the depositor was as exposed as he had ever been, and a good many of the money that mattered was above it.
questions.hint: Ask what the depositor is claiming against before the reform and after it, and whether that is a name or a category.

questions.explanation: The two rates are at different levels and answer to different things. The discount rate is the price the reserve banks charge member banks, and it is the instrument of policy: moving it moves the cost of the marginal borrowing a bank chooses to make, and that is how a common authority reaches a thousand separate lending decisions. The rate a member bank charges its own customer is the price of one loan to one borrower, and no statute can make that a single number without abolishing the judgement about the risk of that loan, which is the thing the district arrangement was designed to preserve. The regulation of the price of credit has always been indirect in this sense, and the confusion between the two rates is the oldest error in the subject. What the act did impose on the member was a set of conditions about what it might do with its money and about what it must be examined for, and a change of a few lines in the statute can make those conditions a great deal stricter or looser.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two rates is a policy instrument and which is a price for one loan to one borrower.

stimulus.body: Original document authored for this bank, not a historical text. From a memorandum on a question submitted by a correspondent: the Act fixes the rate or rates to be charged by the Federal reserve banks on the paper discounted from their members, subject to the approval of the Board of Governors, and to such rate or rates the member banks must pay. The Act does not fix the rate at which a member bank shall lend, nor prescribe what a member may charge a borrower in the ordinary way. What the Act does prescribe is a set of conditions of membership, among them the obligation to maintain reserves, the obligation to permit examination, and restrictions upon the ownership of the stock of member banks by member banks. A member bank is at liberty to make whatever contract with a borrower its judgement approves, subject to those conditions and to the general law.

questions.explanation: A limitation is a statement about what a given kind of evidence can show whatever the facts turn out to be, and that is what the second option is. A before-and-after comparison of a count is consistent with a causal claim and equally consistent with the absence of one, because the world changed in other respects at the same time, and no quantity of arithmetic on the two numbers can remove that. The other three are different in kind. They are claims about the contents and the shape of the record, and each of them is the sort of thing a historian checks before relying on a source: whether a count of issues stands for a count of holdings, whether a published price can be found for a given date, whether a set of minutes is a record of one institution's thinking. Knowing what a source contains is the beginning of using it rather than a limit on it, and confusing the two leads to a peculiar kind of scepticism in which a historian is unwilling to use anything and equally unwilling to say why.
questions.hint: Ask which of these is true whatever the facts of the period turn out to be, and which is a fact about the record.

questions.explanation: The third instruction is about the only asset a bank in that position actually has, which is the belief of the people who have left money with it. A suspension of payment on demand is, from the point of view of a depositor, the bank saying the money may not be there; silence makes that message louder, because a depositor who is not told will assume the worst and will act on the assumption, while a depositor who has been told the reason and the plan has something to wait for. The design of paying small sums first is a companion to the same end, since it keeps an ordinary household from being the person who empties the account and frightens the rest. This is the whole argument for disclosure in a crisis, and it also explains why the reform that followed did not simply compel cooperation, which no law could do, but put something behind a deposit so that the disclosure had a subject matter. A bank that can pay its depositors has nothing to explain and nothing to persuade anybody about.

stimulus.body: Original document authored for this bank, not a historical text. From a circular sent to the banks of a city during a banking crisis: you will at once suspend payment on demand deposits. Pay out on small sums rather than on large, so that the ordinary depositor is not the person whose withdrawal alarms the rest. Treat the suspension as temporary and act upon the expectation of resumption. And explain to every depositor who asks, in plain terms and without evasion, what you have done, why you have done it, and upon what you count to resume; a depositor who has been told the truth will wait, and a depositor who has been told nothing will not.

questions.explanation: A and D are the claims a single figure cannot carry, and the reason is the same in both. One failure in one year is one observation, and it can be produced by any of a very large number of causes including fraud, a local crop failure, or the decision of a particular manager, so it cannot establish a property of the whole system. A statute passed in a year of recovery is a coincidence of dates, and a coincidence of dates is a reason to look rather than a conclusion, because recovery follows many things at once. B is a weak but legitimate claim: saying the reform had some part in the fall is a claim about sequence, and sequence is exactly what a before-and-after comparison supplies. C is a bad argument rather than an unprovable one, because it treats a single episode as though it tested a system that it did not test, and it commits the further error of assuming that a system which did not have to act was a system that could not have acted.
questions.hint: Ask in each case whether one observation is being asked to carry a conclusion about a whole system or a whole year.
